A tired cat could still squeeze through; the sentence contrasts tiny with big.
The sentence contrasts tiny with something bigger, not something strange.

plead|sc1.stem: Every night at bedtime, the twins _____ for just one more chapter, saying "Please, please, please!"

decoys.why: Saying please again and again is begging, not pausing before acting.
The twins are begging with words, not working hard to reach a goal.
The twins want to stay for one more chapter, not leave.

plead|sc2.stem: Instead of yelling about a later bedtime, Maya decided to _____ with her parents, softly asking again and again for just ten more minutes.

decoys.why: Maya is asking for ten more minutes, not living somewhere with her parents.
Maya stays and keeps asking softly, so she isn't leaving.

damp|sc1.stem: The beach towel wasn't soaking wet, just a little _____ from drying off after the morning swim.

decoys.why: A towel can't be tired; the clue compares it to soaking wet.
The sentence is about how wet the towel is, not how bright it is.
The clue says not soaking wet, so the blank describes wetness, not strangeness.
Bright colors have nothing to do with drying off; the clue is about wetness.

damp|sc2.stem: The morning dew had left the grass a bit _____, so our socks felt slightly wet by the time we crossed the field to school.

decoys.why: Lively grass wouldn't make your socks wet; the dew made it slightly wet.
The dew affects wetness, not how well the field grows plants.
Bright color wouldn't explain why the socks felt slightly wet.
Stiff grass wouldn't soak socks; the sentence is about dew and wetness.
The grass wasn't hard to find; the dew made it slightly wet.

dim|sc1.stem: The flashlight's batteries were nearly dead, so its beam was too _____ to light the path through the woods.

decoys.why: Nearly dead batteries make a weak beam, and vivid means bright and strong.
The beam couldn't light the path, so it wasn't bright and full of life.
Batteries can run down, but a beam of light can't feel tired.
The beam is on but weak, so the issue is brightness, not being unused.

dim|sc2.stem: The kitchen was bright and sunny at noon, but by evening the light had grown so _____ that Grandma switched on a lamp to read her book.

decoys.why: Grandma needed a lamp, so the light was weak, not bright and strong.
The kitchen was bright at noon but not by evening, so vibrant is backwards.
The light faded so much that Grandma needed a lamp, the opposite of bright.
The blank describes the light, not Grandma, and light can't be tired.
Grandma turned on a lamp because it got dark, not because anything got wet.

fertile|sc1.stem: The farmers chose the valley because its _____ soil could grow huge crops of corn, beans, and squash.

decoys.why: Stiff, hard soil wouldn't grow huge crops of corn, beans, and squash.
The farmers chose the valley for its good soil, not because soil was hard to find.
Worn-out soil couldn't grow huge crops, which is why farmers chose it.
Soil isn't described by brightness; the clue is about growing big crops.
Strange soil doesn't explain why it could grow huge crops.
The crops are huge, but the soil itself is described by how well it grows plants.

fertile|sc2.stem: Nothing would grow in our shady, rocky backyard, but Aunt Rosa's _____ garden produced so many tomatoes that she gave bags of them to the neighbors.

decoys.why: The shady yard grew nothing, so a dim garden wouldn't produce so many tomatoes.
Stiff, hard ground is like the rocky yard, not a garden full of tomatoes.
Aunt Rosa had so many tomatoes she gave them away, the opposite of scarce.
Her garden was busy producing lots of tomatoes, so it wasn't idle.
The sentence describes a garden that grows a lot, not one that seems stern.

weary|sc1.stem: After hearing the same song forty times on the car trip, Dad grew _____ of it and begged us to pick another.

decoys.why: Dad wasn't careful about danger; he heard the song forty times and got tired of it.

weary|sc2.stem: Grandpa usually races us up the hill, but after a whole day of moving furniture, he felt too _____ to climb even the front steps.

decoys.why: Grandpa could not climb even the steps, and vibrant means full of energy.
Wary looks like weary but means watchful of danger, not tired from moving furniture.
Feeling happy would not stop Grandpa from climbing the front steps.
The sentence is about Grandpa being worn out, not about his mood.
Being clever with words has nothing to do with being too worn out to climb.

scarce|sc1.stem: During the long drought, water became so _____ that ten farm families had to share the one well that still worked.

decoys.why: Ten families sharing one well means there was too little water, not more than enough.
Damp is about water, but the sentence is about how little water there was.
Fertile describes land that grows plants, not water that is running out in a drought.
A drought means very little water, so gigantic makes no sense here.
Water cannot be tired; the sentence says there was hardly any water left.

scarce|sc2.stem: In spring the berry bushes were loaded with fruit, but by late fall berries were so _____ that the birds had to search all day to find a few.

decoys.why: The birds searched all day to find a few, so there were not more than enough.
Berries can be bright, but the clue says birds could barely find any.
Fertile describes soil that grows plants, not berries that are hard to find.
Bright color would not make birds search all day to find a few berries.
The problem was how few berries there were, not how big they were.
Wet berries would still be easy to find; the birds found only a few.

cheerful|sc1.stem: The sunny yellow walls and bright curtains made the once-gray waiting room so _____ that even nervous patients smiled.

decoys.why: Sunny yellow walls and bright curtains make a room bright, not dim.
The room made nervous patients smile, so it was not gloomy or stern.
A boring room would not make nervous patients smile.
Nothing in the sentence is about wetness; it is about bright colors making people smile.
A room cannot be tired; the bright colors made it happy looking.

cheerful|sc2.stem: Even though it rained all through our camping trip, my little brother stayed _____, singing silly songs and splashing happily in every puddle.

decoys.why: He was singing silly songs and splashing happily, so he was not stern or gloomy.
Splashing in every puddle shows energy, not being very tired.
Singing silly songs is fun, not long and boring.
Rigid means stiff, but he was happily splashing around in the rain.
He splashed happily in every puddle, so he was not careful about danger.

gracious|sc1.stem: The _____ host greeted every guest warmly at the door, took their coats, and politely offered them lemonade.

decoys.why: The host greeted everyone warmly, so he was not stern and unsmiling.
A host who welcomes every guest warmly is not suspicious of them.
The host was busy taking coats and offering lemonade, not doing nothing.
Nothing in the sentence suggests the host was tired; it shows he was warm and polite.
Rigid means stiff, but the clue is the host's warm and polite welcome.

gracious|sc2.stem: Coach Lee's team lost the championship by one point, yet instead of sulking she was _____, shaking hands with the winners and praising their great game.

decoys.why: Instead of sulking, she praised the winners, so she was not stern and unsmiling.
Rigid means stiff, but the clue is her kind handshakes and praise.
Shaking hands and praising the winners shows kindness, not watching for danger.
She may be tired, but the clue shows her being kind and polite to the winners.
She was actively shaking hands and praising, so she was not doing nothing.

jolly|sc1.stem: The _____ old man in the red suit laughed "Ho, ho, ho!" and handed every child a candy cane.

decoys.why: He laughed and handed out candy canes, so he was not stern and unsmiling.
Laughing "Ho, ho, ho" shows a happy man, not a tired one.
Nothing here is about watching for danger; he was laughing and giving out candy.
A laughing man handing out candy canes is fun, not boring.
Rigid means stiff, but the clue is his happy laugh.

jolly|sc2.stem: Our bus driver is so _____ that his loud laugh and silly jokes turn even the rainiest Monday morning into a fun ride.

decoys.why: A driver with a loud laugh and silly jokes is not stern and unsmiling.
The driver makes the ride fun, so he is not boring.
Loud laughs and silly jokes show energy and happiness, not tiredness.
Rigid means stiff, but the clue is his laughter and jokes.
Silly jokes and laughing have nothing to do with watching for danger.

wary|sc1.stem: The squirrel was _____ of the cat, keeping one eye on it the entire time it nibbled the acorn.

decoys.why: Weary of means tired of; the squirrel was keeping an eye on the cat for safety.

conceal|sc2.stem: The magician's sleeve was so wide that she could easily _____ a whole deck of cards inside it, and the audience never once spotted them.

decoys.why: The sentence is about keeping cards out of sight, not grabbing them suddenly.
The audience never spotted the cards, so the point is hiding them, not loving them.
The sleeve holds cards so nobody sees them; failing to care for cards makes no sense.
Nothing in the sentence is about fear; the clue is that nobody spotted the cards.
You cannot understand cards inside a sleeve; the clue says she kept them hidden.

boast|sc1.stem: Kenji likes to _____ about his video game scores, telling everyone again and again how great he is.

decoys.why: Kenji tells everyone again and again, so he is not pausing at all.

boast|sc2.stem: Because Theo would _____ about his new sneakers all day long, his friends rolled their eyes and said, 'We get it, your shoes are the best.'

decoys.why: Theo talked about his sneakers all day long, which is the opposite of pausing.

prohibit|sc1.stem: The museum's rules strictly _____ visitors from touching the paintings or taking flash photos.

prohibit|sc2.stem: At home I can eat snacks anywhere, but my school's rules _____ eating in the library, so I always finish my apple before I go inside.

decoys.why: You finish your apple before going inside, so the rules do not allow eating there.
Rules that ignore eating would let you snack inside, but you finish your apple first.
The rules stop eating in the library; they do not hide it.
Rules cannot fear anything; the sentence shows they do not allow eating in the library.

tedious|sc1.stem: Copying all one hundred spelling words by hand five times was _____, taking hours of slow, boring work.

decoys.why: The sentence calls the work slow and boring, which is the opposite of cheerful.
Hours of slow, boring work is not happy and cheerful.
You might feel tired after copying, but the work itself is boring, not tired.
Copying words by hand is boring work, not something clever and funny.
Slow, boring work is the opposite of bright and full of life.

tedious|sc2.stem: The first part of the movie was full of car chases, but the last hour was so _____ that my little brother fell asleep on the couch.

decoys.why: Your brother fell asleep, so the last hour was dull, not full of life.
Your brother was tired, but the movie itself was boring, not tired.
A clever, funny movie would keep him awake, but he fell asleep.
The clue is that he fell asleep, which points to boring, not happy and bright.

radiant|sc1.stem: When she saw her long-lost cousin at the gate, Aisha's face was _____, glowing with happiness like the morning sun.

decoys.why: Aisha was glowing with happiness, not serious and quiet.
A face glowing like the morning sun is the opposite of cold and cheerless.
The sentence says her face was glowing, and dim means not bright.
She was glowing with happiness at seeing her cousin, not very tired.
Aisha was overjoyed to see her cousin, not watchful about danger.

radiant|sc2.stem: After weeks of gray, rainy skies, the garden looked _____ when the sun finally came out and lit up every wet leaf and petal.

decoys.why: Bleak fits the gray weeks, but the sun finally came out and lit everything up.
The sun lit up every leaf, so the garden was bright, not dim.
The sentence is about sunlight making the garden shine, not looking serious and quiet.
The clue is the sun lighting up every leaf, which is about glowing, not neatness.
The garden was lit up by sunshine, not very tired.

mimic|sc1.stem: The mockingbird can _____ car alarms, other birds, and even barking dogs, copying each sound perfectly.

decoys.why: The sentence says the bird copies each sound perfectly, not that it fears them.
The clue is copying each sound, not understanding car alarms or dogs.
The bird copies the sounds; nothing says it loves car alarms or barking dogs.
The bird copies sounds perfectly, which is the opposite of hiding them.
A bird cannot forbid car alarms by rule; the sentence says it copies them.

wary|sc2.stem: Most of the ducks swam right up for bread, but one old duck stayed _____, circling at a distance and watching our hands before it came close.

decoys.why: Weary means tired, but the duck was circling and watching your hands, which shows caution.

Nothing says the duck was happy; it stayed back and watched carefully before coming close.
The sentence describes a duck being careful about danger, not one feeling happy and bright.
The duck was busy circling and watching, so it was not sitting idle.

witty|sc1.stem: Known for her _____ remarks, Jasmine could make the whole class laugh with one clever line.

decoys.why: Boring remarks would not make the whole class laugh with one clever line.
Stern, unsmiling remarks would not get the class laughing.
Cheerless remarks would not make anyone laugh, and the sentence calls her lines clever.
Wary looks like witty but means careful about danger, which has nothing to do with jokes.
Tired remarks would not be the clever lines that made the class laugh.
The sentence says her lines were clever, not awkward.

witty|sc2.stem: The movie's jokes were flat and boring, but the talking parrot's _____ comebacks had everyone in the theater laughing at how clever they were.

decoys.why: Tedious describes the movie's boring jokes, but the parrot's comebacks were the clever contrast.
Stern, unsmiling comebacks would not have the whole theater laughing.
Cheerless comebacks would not make everyone laugh at how clever they were.
Wary means careful about danger, but the sentence is about clever, funny comebacks.
Tired comebacks would not be the clever ones that got the theater laughing.
The audience laughed at how clever the comebacks were, not how awkward.

fragment|sc1.stem: While digging in the garden, Lucas found a small _____ of a broken clay pot with blue paint on it.

decoys.why: Lucas found a broken piece of a pot, not something blocking his way.
The sentence describes a small piece of a clay pot, not a danger.
A blunder is a mistake, but Lucas found a physical piece of a broken pot.
A small dwelling is a home, not something that comes from a broken clay pot.
A triumph is a win, not a piece of a broken pot you dig up.
Nothing in the sentence is being cured; Lucas found a broken piece of a pot.

fragment|sc2.stem: When the old plate slipped off the table and shattered, Dad picked up every sharp _____ from the floor so no one would cut a foot.

decoys.why: Dropping the plate was a mistake, but Dad picked up sharp pieces from the floor.

tidy|sc1.stem: Unlike her brother's messy room, Jada's room is _____, with books lined up on shelves and clothes folded in drawers.

Lined-up books and folded clothes show order, not brightness or liveliness.

tidy|sc2.stem: Because Grandma likes everything in its place, she keeps her kitchen _____, wiping every counter and putting each spoon back in the same drawer.

decoys.why: Wiping counters might leave them wet, but the clue is that she likes everything in its place.
Putting each spoon back in its drawer is about order, not about how bright the kitchen is.
The sentence describes how neat Grandma keeps her kitchen, not how big it is.
Grandma keeps things in their place, which is about neatness, not fancy or costly decoration.

Wiping counters and putting spoons away make a kitchen neat, not strong and solid.

cherish|sc1.stem: Abuela will always _____ the quilt her mother sewed, keeping it safe and loving it more than anything she owns.

decoys.why: The sentence says she keeps the quilt safe and loves it, the opposite of neglecting it.

You endure something hard, but Abuela loves this quilt more than anything she owns.
She keeps the quilt safe, so she is not using it up.

cherish|sc2.stem: Leo thought the old seashell was just junk, but his little sister will _____ it forever because their grandfather found it on his last beach trip.

decoys.why: Leo thought it was junk, but the word but shows his sister feels the opposite.

conceal|sc1.stem: Max tried to _____ the broken lamp by throwing a blanket over it so that no one would see it.

decoys.why: Max threw the blanket on so no one would see the lamp, which means hiding it.

mimic|sc2.stem: Instead of inventing her own dance for the talent show, Lily chose to _____ her favorite pop star, matching every spin and hand wave.

glee|sc1.stem: Squealing with _____, the twins raced outside to build their very first snowman.

glee|sc2.stem: Mia expected to feel nervous on the roller coaster, but instead she screamed with _____ the whole ride and begged to go again.

accumulate|sc1.stem: If you never sweep under the bed, dust bunnies will slowly _____ there, piling higher over the months.

Piling higher means building up on the floor, not flying high in the air.

accumulate|sc2.stem: Because Jamal saved every quarter he found for two years, enough coins began to _____ in his jar to buy a new skateboard.

decoys.why: Jamal saved every quarter, so his coins built up instead of disappearing.

roam|sc1.stem: On the big ranch, the horses are free to _____ across hundreds of acres with no fences to stop them.

roam|sc2.stem: At the zoo the lions stay in small pens, but in the wild they _____ for miles across the grassy plains, going wherever they please.

clumsy|sc1.stem: Usually graceful on the ice, Nora felt _____ in her new skates, wobbling and bumping into the wall all afternoon.

decoys.why: Nora was wobbling and bumping the wall, so she was not steady and solid.

clumsy|sc2.stem: Because his feet had grown so fast that summer, Leo became _____ and kept tripping over chairs and knocking cups off the table.

decoys.why: Leo kept tripping over chairs, so he was not steady and solid.

Tripping over chairs is accidental, not tricky or sneaky.

sturdy|sc1.stem: Unlike the wobbly card table, the _____ oak bench held all five of us without a single creak.

Holding five people without a creak shows the bench is strong, not neat.

sturdy|sc2.stem: The little bridge over the creek was so _____ that even when the whole class marched across it at once, it never swayed or cracked.

bleak|sc1.stem: In winter the island is _____, with icy winds, bare gray rocks, and not a single flower to cheer anyone up.

decoys.why: The island has not a single flower, so it cannot be full of growing plants.

Icy winds and bare gray rocks are not shining or glowing.

bleak|sc2.stem: In June the old park bursts with roses and laughing children, but by January it looks _____, with leafless trees and empty, frozen benches.

Empty, frozen benches are bare, not rich and fancy.

lavish|sc1.stem: The prince's birthday party was _____, with a chocolate fountain, gold plates, and a hired orchestra that cost a fortune.

decoys.why: Gold plates and a chocolate fountain are the opposite of bare and cheerless.

The party had plenty of fancy things, so it was not in short supply.
Rough to the touch has nothing to do with a party that cost a fortune.
The clue is about cost and fanciness, not about being high or towering.
Strong and solid does not describe gold plates and a hired orchestra.

lavish|sc2.stem: Our class picnic was usually just sandwiches on a blanket, but this year a parent planned a _____ feast with silver trays, fancy cakes, and a magician.

decoys.why: Silver trays, fancy cakes, and a magician are not bare or cheerless.

Rough to the touch does not describe silver trays and fancy cakes.
A feast with a magician is not dark or hopeless.

The clue is about fancy, costly treats, not about being strong and solid.

coarse|sc1.stem: Unlike the smooth silk scarf, the burlap sack felt _____ and scratchy against Rosa's skin.

decoys.why: Silk sounds fancy, but the blank describes how the burlap felt: scratchy.

The blank tells how burlap feels, not whether it is hard to find.

coarse|sc2.stem: Dad chose the _____ sandpaper for the splintery fence, because its big, gritty grains would scrape the wood down fast.

decoys.why: The sandpaper has big, gritty grains, which says rough, not fancy and costly.

solemn|sc1.stem: The ceremony was _____: no one spoke or smiled as the flag was slowly raised in the quiet morning air.

decoys.why: No one smiled, so the ceremony could not be happy and cheerful.

The clue is the silence and seriousness, not fancy or costly things.

solemn|sc2.stem: During the school's moment of silence for the veterans, the usually giggly kindergartners became _____, standing still with their hands folded.

sly|sc1.stem: With a _____ grin, Max sneakily slipped the last cookie into his pocket when no one was looking.

sly|sc2.stem: Everyone thought the new puppy was too sweet to cause trouble, but it was actually quite _____, secretly hiding shoes whenever we turned our backs.

Solemn means serious and quiet, which does not explain secretly hiding shoes.

peril|sc1.stem: When they heard the ice cracking beneath them, the skaters knew they were in _____ and hurried back to shore.

peril|sc2.stem: Unlike the calm pond where we swim safely, the rushing river below the waterfall puts swimmers in real _____, so lifeguards never let anyone go there.

gloomy|sc1.stem: On that _____ afternoon, dark clouds hid the sun and everyone in the cabin felt sad and hopeless about the canceled hike.

gloomy|sc2.stem: Even though her best friend was moving away, Lily refused to stay _____ for long; by dinner she was cheerfully planning video calls.

soar|sc1.stem: Hawks _____ high above the canyon, gliding on warm air for hours without flapping their wings.

soar|sc2.stem: Because the wind was strong and steady at the beach, our new kite could finally _____ above the waves instead of crashing into the sand.

To trudge is to walk heavily, but a supply of snacks does not walk; it shrinks.
To glisten is to shine, which has nothing to do with snacks running out.

dwindle|sc2.stem: At first, hundreds of fans waited outside the stadium for autographs, but as the cold night went on, the crowd began to _____ until only a few were left.

decoys.why: Arguing would not make hundreds of fans shrink down to only a few.
The cold might make fans huddle, but the sentence says the crowd got smaller until few remained.
Putting off leaving would keep the crowd large, but the sentence says only a few were left.
Crying out does not explain how hundreds of fans became only a few.
To glisten is to shine, and the sentence is about the crowd getting smaller.

tactful|sc1.stem: Not wanting to hurt Grandma's feelings, Lily gave a _____ answer about the itchy sweater Grandma had knitted for her.

decoys.why: Lily did not want to hurt Grandma's feelings, and a haughty answer would be proud and rude.
A gloomy, angry answer would hurt Grandma, which is exactly what Lily wanted to avoid.
A very sad answer would not protect Grandma's feelings about the sweater she knitted.
A sorrowful answer would make Grandma feel bad, but Lily wanted to spare her feelings.
Sounding discouraged would hurt Grandma, and the sentence says Lily wanted to avoid that.
Scrawny means thin and bony, which describes a body, not a kind answer.

tactful|sc2.stem: Instead of laughing at Ben's terrible haircut like the others did, Ana was _____ and said only that it would grow back soon.

decoys.why: Ana avoided mocking Ben and spoke kindly, so she was not proud and looking down on him.
The others were laughing gleefully, but the sentence says Ana did not join them.
Nothing was being celebrated; Ana was gently trying not to hurt Ben's feelings.
Ana spoke kindly about the haircut growing back, not in a gloomy, angry way.
Being very hungry has nothing to do with how Ana responded to Ben's haircut.

bicker|sc1.stem: The twins always _____ over silly things, like who gets the window seat or the bigger slice of pizza.

decoys.why: The twins fight over seats and pizza, which is arguing, not just crying out suddenly.
Putting things off does not fit fighting over who gets the window seat.
To scamper is to run lightly, but the twins are fighting over seats and pizza slices.
To glisten is to shine, which has nothing to do with fighting over pizza.
The twins are not getting smaller; they are arguing over silly things.

bicker|sc2.stem: At school, Leo and Sam are best friends who share everything, but at home the brothers _____ about whose turn it is to feed the dog.

decoys.why: The word but shows the brothers stop getting along at home, so they argue, not just cry out.
Running around does not contrast with being best friends; arguing about the dog does.
Wandering slowly does not show the brothers disagreeing about whose turn it is.
Walking heavily does not fit a disagreement about whose turn it is to feed the dog.

illegible|sc1.stem: Dr. Patel's handwriting was so _____ that the pharmacist could not read a single word on the note.

decoys.why: Scrawny sounds like scrawl but means thin and bony, not too messy to read.
Handwriting cannot be careful about feelings; the pharmacist simply could not read it.
Lethargic means tired and slow, but the clue is that no word could be read.
Cheerful handwriting would not stop the pharmacist from reading a single word.
Handwriting cannot be proud; the sentence says the note was impossible to read.

illegible|sc2.stem: Unlike her neat, careful printing in third grade, Maya's rushed notes this year were so _____ that even she couldn't figure out what she had written.

decoys.why: Scrawny sounds like scrawl but means thin and bony, not too messy to read.
Hardworking notes would not be impossible to read; the sentence says Maya could not read them.
Notes cannot be careful about feelings; the problem is that Maya could not read them.
Thoughtful notes would not explain why Maya could not figure out her own writing.
The notes were rushed, not slow and tired, and the clue is that they were unreadable.

cower|sc1.stem: During thunderstorms, our puppy would _____ under the kitchen table, crouching low with its tail tucked between its legs.

decoys.why: The puppy is crouching low in one spot, not wandering slowly around.
A puppy with its tail tucked is scared, not rudely making fun of anyone.
The puppy is hiding from the storm in fear, not wasting time.
Nobody is arguing here; the puppy is crouching alone in fear.
The sentence is about the puppy's fear of thunder, not shining.
The puppy is crouching low under the table, not walking heavily.

cower|sc2.stem: My little brother acts brave all day, but when the lights go out, he will _____ under his blanket until Dad checks the closet for monsters.

decoys.why: The brother is scared of the dark, not making fun of anyone.
He is hiding alone under his blanket, not arguing with anyone.
The word but shows his bravery disappears; he is scared, not wasting time.
He stays hidden under his blanket, so he is not wandering anywhere.
He is quietly hiding in fear, not crying out suddenly.
The sentence is about being afraid of monsters, not shining.

gleeful|sc1.stem: With a _____ giggle, Toby watched his snowball sail over the fence and land right on his big brother's hat.

decoys.why: Toby's snowball hit its target, so his giggle is happy, not sad.
A giggle at a perfect snowball throw is delighted, not gloomy and angry.
Toby succeeded with his snowball, so he is not discouraged.
Landing a snowball on his brother's hat makes Toby happy, not sad.
A giggle is playful, not quiet and deep in thought.
Toby is giggling and throwing snowballs, so he is not tired and slow.

gleeful|sc2.stem: When the principal announced that summer vacation would start a day early, the _____ students cheered, hugged, and danced right out the classroom door.

decoys.why: The students cheered and danced, so they were happy, not discouraged.
Students who cheer and hug are delighted, not quietly angry.
An early vacation made them cheer, so they were not full of sadness.
Students who danced out the door had lots of energy.
Cheering and dancing show joy, not sadness.
Students who cheer and dance are not quietly lost in thought.

trudge|sc1.stem: Tired after school, the kids had to _____ home through the deep, wet snow, their heavy boots dragging with each step.

decoys.why: Tired kids with dragging boots move slowly and heavily, not quickly and lightly.
The wet snow might shine, but the sentence is about how the kids walked.

trudge|sc2.stem: In the morning we raced to the beach, but after a long afternoon in the hot sun, we had to _____ back to the car with our heavy bags.

decoys.why: The word but shows they slowed down; heavy bags rule out running lightly.

famished|sc1.stem: Having skipped lunch to finish his art project, Diego felt _____ by dinner and wolfed down three plates of pasta.

decoys.why: Wolfing down three plates after skipping lunch shows hunger, not celebration.
The clue is skipping lunch, which makes him hungry, not delighted.
Eating three plates of pasta shows hunger, not quiet thinking.
Nothing here shows pride; skipping lunch made Diego hungry.
The sentence is about skipping lunch and eating a lot, not being polite.
Diego wolfed down pasta because he was hungry, not because he was stubborn.

famished|sc2.stem: Although Mia had eaten a huge breakfast, by the end of the long hike she was so _____ that she ate two sandwiches and a whole bag of apples.

decoys.why: Being thin is not why she ate so much; the long hike made her hungry.
Eating two sandwiches and a bag of apples shows hunger, not cheerfulness.
Being delighted would not make her eat so much food after a hike.
Thinking deeply does not explain eating two sandwiches and a bag of apples.
Being polite has nothing to do with eating a huge amount after a hike.
Pride does not explain eating so much; the long hike made her hungry.

beckon|sc1.stem: From across the playground, Grandpa gave a little wave of his hand to _____ us over for lunch.

beckon|sc2.stem: When the lifeguard spotted us swimming too far out, she began to _____ us back toward shore, waving her arms until we swam closer.
